The core derivation begins with the Kelly criterion’s application to financial returns, which requires a well-defined probability distribution. Standard normal distributions are unsuitable due to unbounded extremes, leading to invalid Kelly fractions when returns approach infinity. To resolve this, a quasi-normal distribution is introduced, defined over a finite interval [A, B]. This truncation ensures boundedness and enables meaningful computation of the Kelly optimal fraction. The normalization constant h adjusts the density so that total probability remains unity within the interval. These primitives form a dual structure: one for probabilistic modeling (truncated normal), and another for decision optimization (Kelly constraint). Failure modes arise when the truncation bounds are too narrow or when the underlying distribution deviates significantly from normality. The system must maintain consistency across layers—GSI for inference, GSE for action selection.
